stimulus.title: Drill C1 · Ciências naturais · alvo: 6 min
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Bioluminescence in Marine Organisms

Bioluminescence (the production and emission of light by a living organism) is remarkably common in the ocean, appearing in bacteria, jellyfish, fish, and even some sharks. Unlike the light produced by an incandescent bulb, which wastes most of its energy as heat, bioluminescent light is generated through a highly efficient chemical reaction, typically involving a light-emitting molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. Because so little energy is lost as heat, biologists sometimes refer to this phenomenon as "cold light."

The functions of bioluminescence vary considerably across species, though three purposes appear again and again. Some organisms use light defensively: certain species of squid release a luminous cloud instead of ink, startling predators and buying time to escape. Others use it as a hunting tool. The anglerfish, perhaps the most famous example, dangles a glowing lure above its mouth to attract smaller prey close enough to seize. Still others use light for communication. In the deep sea, darkness is nearly absolute, so visual signals cannot rely on ambient light at all. Even in shallow water at night, certain ostracods, tiny crustaceans, produce synchronized light displays to attract mates.

What makes bioluminescence especially interesting to evolutionary biologists is that it did not evolve just once. Genetic and biochemical evidence indicates that the capacity for bioluminescence has arisen independently dozens of times across unrelated lineages, using different chemical pathways to achieve a similar outcome. This pattern, in which unrelated organisms evolve similar traits independently, is known as convergent evolution, and bioluminescence is considered one of its most striking examples.

prompt: Ideia principal. What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Bioluminescence is a rare adaptation found only in a few deep-sea species.
options.B: Bioluminescence is a widespread, chemically efficient trait that serves multiple functions and evolved independently many times.
options.C: The anglerfish, which uses a glowing lure to catch its prey, is the most important example of bioluminescence.
options.D: Bioluminescent light is less efficient than artificial light because much of its energy is lost as heat.

explanation: Cobre os três eixos (o que é + eficiência, funções, evolução independente). (A) contradiz "remarkably common"; (C) é detalhe, e o texto diz "perhaps the most famous", não "o mais importante"; (D) inverte a comparação com a lâmpada.

stimulus.title: Drill C2 · História · alvo: 6 min
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Coffee Houses in Seventeenth-Century England

The first English coffee house opened in Oxford in 1650; within two decades, London alone had hundreds. [■A] For the price of a single cup (a penny), a customer could sit for hours, read the newspapers provided by the house, and join whatever conversation was underway. [■B] Because admission was cheap and open to any man who could pay, the coffee house mixed people who rarely met elsewhere: merchants, scholars, clergymen, and minor gentry sat at the same long tables. [■C]

This mixing had consequences that reached well beyond casual talk. Particular houses became known for particular subjects. Men interested in maritime insurance gathered at Lloyd's; those following scientific debates went to the houses near the Royal Society. [■D] Information that had once circulated slowly, by letter or rumor, now moved quickly through these rooms. Some historians argue that the coffee house functioned as an early public sphere: a space where opinion could form through discussion rather than being handed down by church or crown.

The authorities were not comfortable with this. In 1675, the king issued a proclamation ordering the coffee houses closed, on the grounds that they spread "false, malicious and scandalous reports." The order provoked such immediate opposition that it was withdrawn within days. The houses continued to operate for another century, gradually giving way to private clubs and, eventually, to the institutions that had first taken shape around their tables.

stimulus.title: Drill C3 · Ciências sociais · alvo: 6 min
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: The Strength of Weak Ties

When people look for a new job, common sense suggests they should turn to their closest contacts: family and good friends who know them well and want to help. In a study of professionals who had recently changed jobs, the sociologist Mark Granovetter found the opposite. Of those who had found their new position through a personal contact, most had heard about it not from a close friend but from an acquaintance — someone they saw only occasionally and would not have described as part of their inner circle.

Granovetter's explanation rests on how information moves through social networks. Your close friends tend to know one another and to move in the same circles you do. As a result, they are exposed to more or less the same information you already have; what they can tell you, you have often already heard. An acquaintance, by contrast, moves in a different circle, encounters different people, and hears different news. A weak tie is therefore a bridge to parts of the network you could not otherwise reach.

The finding has been extended well beyond job-hunting. Weak ties have been linked to the spread of new ideas between organizations, to the circulation of information during emergencies, and to innovation within companies, where teams connected to many outside groups tend to produce more original work. Critics note that weak ties are not always advantageous: they carry less trust, and acting on information from a near-stranger involves more risk. But the core insight has held up: the contacts most likely to tell you something genuinely new are often the ones you know least well.

prompt: Ideia principal. The main idea of the passage is that:

options.A: close friends are usually the most reliable source of job leads, since they know us well and want to help
options.B: weak ties often supply new information because they link us to other parts of a network
options.C: social networks have no effect on how people find jobs
options.D: Granovetter's study has been completely disproved

explanation: Tese central: weak ties frequentemente trazem informação mais nova porque conectam a outras partes da rede. (A) contradiz o achado; (C)/(D) distorcem.

When people look for a new job, common sense suggests they should turn to their closest contacts: family and good friends who know them well and want to help. In a study of professionals who had recently changed jobs, the sociologist Mark Granovetter found the opposite. Of those who had found their new position through a personal contact, most had heard about it not from a close friend but from an acquaintance — someone they saw only occasionally and would not have described as part of their inner circle.

Granovetter's explanation rests on how information moves through social networks. Your close friends tend to know one another and to move in the same circles you do. As a result, they are exposed to more or less the same information you already have; what they can tell you, you have often already heard. An acquaintance, by contrast, moves in a different circle, encounters different people, and hears different news. A weak tie is therefore a bridge to parts of the network you could not otherwise reach.

The finding has been extended well beyond job-hunting. Weak ties have been linked to the spread of new ideas between organizations, to the circulation of information during emergencies, and to innovation within companies, where teams connected to many outside groups tend to produce more original work. Critics note that weak ties are not always advantageous: they carry less trust, and acting on information from a near-stranger involves more risk. But the core insight has held up: the contacts most likely to tell you something genuinely new are often the ones you know least well.

options.A: is completely new to us
options.B: we have often already heard
options.C: is always more trustworthy and therefore more useful
options.D: comes from distant parts of the network that we cannot reach ourselves

explanation: "They are exposed to more or less the same information you already have; what they can tell you, you have often already heard." (D) descreve os conhecidos, não os amigos próximos.

stimulus.title: Bloco C: Read an Academic Passage (versão abreviada)
stimulus.content:
**PASSAGE: Coral Bleaching and Thermal Stress**

Coral reefs, despite occupying less than one percent of the ocean floor, support roughly a quarter of all known marine species. This disproportionate biodiversity depends on a delicate symbiotic relationship between coral polyps and microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which live within coral tissue and supply the majority of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. When ocean temperatures rise even slightly above a coral's tolerance threshold: often by as little as one or two degrees Celsius sustained over several weeks · the algae are expelled, leaving the coral's white calcium carbonate skeleton visible. This phenomenon, known as bleaching, does not itself kill the coral immediately, but it severs the primary energy supply, leaving the organism vulnerable to starvation and disease. Recovery is possible if temperatures normalize quickly, but repeated bleaching events, now increasingly common under sustained ocean warming, leave reefs with progressively less time to recover between episodes.

prompt: According to the passage, zooxanthellae primarily provide coral with:

options.A: protection from predators
options.B: energy through photosynthesis
options.C: structural support for the skeleton
options.D: resistance to temperature change

stimulus.title: Bloco C: Read an Academic Passage (versão abreviada)
stimulus.content:
**PASSAGE 2: The Printing Press and the Standardization of Language**

Before the spread of print in fifteenth-century Europe, a single language could vary so much from region to region that speakers a few hundred kilometers apart struggled to read one another's writing. Scribes copied texts by hand, and each copy absorbed the copyist's own spelling habits, regional vocabulary, and errors. There was no strong pressure toward a single written standard, because the audience for any given manuscript was small and usually local.

The printing press changed the economics of this situation. A printer who set a book in type was making a substantial investment and needed to sell copies across as wide an area as possible to recover the cost. This gave printers a direct financial incentive to choose forms of spelling and grammar that the largest number of readers would accept. Over several decades, the dialect of the commercially dominant region (often the capital or the largest trading city) tended to become the basis of the printed standard, not because it was linguistically superior, but because it reached the biggest market.

This standardizing effect was not entirely welcome. Writers who spoke regional varieties found their own usage increasingly marked as incorrect, and forms of the language that were never printed came to be seen as mere "dialect" rather than legitimate versions of the language. Many historians of language now argue that the "standard" form of many European languages owes less to any natural center of the language than to which city happened to dominate early commercial printing.

options.B: how commercial pressures in early printing shaped which form of a language became "standard"

stimulus.title: Bloco C: Read an Academic Passage (alvo: 12–14 min)
stimulus.content:
**PASSAGE: The Economics of Network Effects**

A network effect occurs when the value of a product or service increases as more people use it. The telephone is the textbook example: a single telephone is useless, but as adoption grows, each additional user increases the value of the network for everyone already connected to it. This dynamic, largely peripheral to economic theory for much of the twentieth century, has become central to understanding digital markets, where platforms (social networks, marketplaces, operating systems) often derive their value primarily from the size and engagement of their user base rather than from the intrinsic quality of the underlying product.

Network effects can be direct or indirect. Direct network effects occur when the value to a user increases as a function of other users of the *same* product: a messaging app is more useful as more of one's contacts join it. Indirect network effects occur across two distinct but interdependent user groups: a ride-sharing platform becomes more attractive to riders as more drivers join, and simultaneously more attractive to drivers as more riders join. This two-sided dynamic creates a powerful feedback loop that, once initiated, can be extraordinarily difficult for competitors to disrupt.

This difficulty of disruption is often described as a "winner-take-most" dynamic. Because users generally prefer the platform with the largest existing network, early leaders in markets with strong network effects tend to compound their advantage rapidly, often achieving dominant market positions that persist even when competitors offer superior underlying technology. This has generated significant regulatory concern, particularly regarding whether dominant platforms leverage network-effect-driven market power in ways that stifle competition rather than simply reflecting superior efficiency.

Critics of this narrative, however, caution against treating network effects as an insurmountable barrier to entry. History offers counterexamples: several dominant platforms have been displaced by newer entrants offering a sufficiently differentiated experience, suggesting that network effects, while powerful, are not absolute. Low switching costs, multi-homing behavior (where users maintain accounts on multiple competing platforms simultaneously), and shifts in user preference can erode even substantial network advantages over time.

options.B: To explain the concept of network effects and evaluate the extent of their competitive power
options.C: To criticize regulators for failing to break up dominant technology platforms
options.D: To describe the history of the telephone as a communication technology

Because users generally prefer the platform with the largest existing network, early leaders in markets with strong network effects tend to compound their advantage rapidly, often achieving dominant market positions that persist even when competitors offer superior underlying technology. This has generated significant regulatory concern, particularly regarding whether dominant platforms leverage network-effect-driven market power in ways that stifle competition rather than simply reflecting superior efficiency.

Critics of this narrative, however, caution against treating network effects as an insurmountable barrier to entry. Low switching costs, multi-homing behavior (where users maintain accounts on multiple competing platforms simultaneously), and shifts in user preference can erode even substantial network advantages over time.
